newsitem.title: USA: Indian consumption seen driving 1996 silver demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian consumption seen driving 1996 silver demand.

text.p: A surge in Indian silver demand during the second half of 1996 led to a drawdown in above-ground world silver stocks, according to premliminary data from Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS).

"The data for India looked so significant and surprising, we thought we would provide an indication now, rather than wait until May," GFMS chief executive Stewart Murray said in an interview with Reuters.
GFMS is collecting data for the Silver Institute's 1997 silver survey due to be published in May.

For 1996 as a whole, total silver imports through India's two officials channels amounted to just over 100 million ounces, representing a rise of more than 30 percent from 1995, GFMS chief executive Stewart Murray said.
"India's current impact on the world market has been remarkable," Murray said.
"After a generation in which it was essentially a dishoarder of the metal, it has imported more than 500 million ounces in the last seven years."

The increase in Indian silver demand followed good harvests which boosted consumer demand, especially in the Northern tribal belts where heavyweight silver jewelry remains the favored method of saving among rural populations, Murray said.
The rise in Indian demand occurred despite a rise in the year's average price in rupee terms of six percent.
But the fall in silver prices later in the year helped accelerate the pace of imports from 13 million ounces in the first quarter to a new record of almost 35 million ounces in the fourth quarter.

In Thailand a number of silver manufacturers look to be recovering from the depressed conditions of 1995, when fabrication demand fell more than four percent from the 1994 level. Thailand's exports of silver jewelry to the US increased significantly last year, Murray said.

In the US, although fabrication of silverware was stable in 1996, jewelry demand continued to advance, with imports from Mexico and Italy the highlight, though final data for 1996 is not yet available because as much as 40 percent of all jewelry sold in the US is sold during the Christmas holiday period.
But industrial silver use in the US last year was mixed, with a decline in demand from the semi-conductor industry offset by growth from other products.

On the supply side, mine production in North America appeared to fall, with output from McCoy Cove and Grouse Creek down sharply, offsetting increased output from the Candelaria mine and the reopened Coeur and Galena mines.
However, "we have no reason to suspect that the ongoing deficit between silver supply and demand deficit has changed significantly," Murray said.
"We would have had to have large falls elsewhere to offset the increase we are seeing in Indian demand for the drawdown in inventories to have halted."

Since 1989 the amount of silver used by fabricators in the manufacture of jewelry, silverware, silverplate, photographic film and paper and other products, has exceeded the flow of silver refined from mine production, old scrapped items and other sources, leading to a large drawdown in world silver inventories.
